title: Biochemistry — Mixed Exam Formats (DOMiNANCE Originals)
source: KNUST Biochemistry lectures and corresponding study guides

questions.stem:
Assertion: Light hyperpolarizes rod photoreceptors.
Reason: Activated cGMP phosphodiesterase closes cGMP-gated cation channels by lowering cGMP.
questions.why: Light activates rhodopsin and its transducin–phosphodiesterase cascade. The resulting fall in cGMP closes inward cation channels and reduces the depolarising dark current, explaining the rod's hyperpolarisation.

notes.B: A decrease in inward cation current is precisely what makes the membrane potential more negative.
notes.C: Activated phosphodiesterase lowers cGMP, which normally helps hold the cation channels open.
notes.D: Illumination does produce a graded hyperpolarisation by reducing the inward dark current.
notes.E: Both the rod hyperpolarisation and the decrease in cGMP leading to channel closure occur in phototransduction.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Vitamin A deficiency can impair dark adaptation.
Reason: Rod photoreceptors function only under bright illumination.
questions.why: Vitamin A deficiency can limit retinal supply and delay the regeneration of rod rhodopsin. This impairs dark adaptation because rods are specialised for dim-light vision.

notes.A: Vitamin A deficiency can impair dark adaptation, but the bright-light-only claim about rods is false.
notes.B: The two statements are not both true because rods are most useful at low light levels.
notes.D: Inadequate availability of retinal can impair dark adaptation, and rods do not function exclusively under bright illumination.
notes.E: The statement about rods is false, but the vitamin A deficiency can indeed compromise visual-pigment regeneration.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Scurvy causes defective collagen triple-helix stability.
Reason: Ascorbate supports ferrous iron-dependent prolyl hydroxylation.
questions.why: Ascorbate helps maintain the ferrous iron needed for collagen prolyl hydroxylase. Vitamin C deficiency limits formation of hydroxyproline, which normally helps collagen helices remain stable at body temperature.

notes.B: The ascorbate requirement is the link between dietary deficiency, reduced hydroxyproline formation and loss of helix stability.
notes.C: Ascorbate does support the activity of iron-dependent collagen prolyl hydroxylase.
notes.D: The collagen helix can be less stable in scurvy because sufficient hydroxylated proline is unavailable.
notes.E: Both the hydroxylation role of ascorbate and the resulting defect in scurvy are established.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Lysyl oxidase requires ferrous iron to form allysine.
Reason: Prolyl hydroxylase requires copper to form hydroxyproline.
questions.why: The metal requirements are reversed. Lysyl oxidase requires copper to produce reactive lysine-derived aldehydes, whereas collagen prolyl hydroxylase requires ferrous iron to produce hydroxyproline.

notes.A: Neither metal assignment is correct. Lysyl oxidase uses copper and prolyl hydroxylase uses ferrous iron.
notes.B: The claims do not describe two valid independent facts, since both enzymes are assigned the other's metal.
notes.C: The assertion is false because the cofactor of lysyl oxidase is copper rather than ferrous iron.
notes.D: The reason is false because collagen prolyl hydroxylase uses ferrous iron rather than copper.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Maternal IgG can cross the placenta.
Reason: IgM is usually the first major antibody class produced during a primary response.
questions.why: Both statements are true. Placental FcRn selectively transports maternal IgG, whereas early IgM production describes the kinetics of a primary antibody response and does not explain placental transport.

notes.A: The timing of IgM production does not explain transport of IgG across the placenta by FcRn.
notes.C: IgM commonly appears early during primary immune responses, so the reason is true.
notes.D: Maternal IgG does cross the placenta through receptor-mediated transport, so the assertion is true.
notes.E: Both early IgM production and transplacental IgG transport are real, independent immune phenomena.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Type IV hypersensitivity is principally antibody-mediated.
Reason: Th1 cytokines may activate macrophages in delayed-type inflammation.
questions.why: Type IV hypersensitivity depends principally on sensitised T cells, so the assertion is false. In a classic delayed response, Th1 cells produce signals that activate tissue macrophages.

notes.A: Type IV hypersensitivity is T-cell-mediated, so the claim of primary antibody mediation is false.
notes.B: The assertion incorrectly describes antibody-mediated injury, while type IV responses are driven by sensitised T cells.
notes.C: Th1 cytokines can indeed enhance macrophage activation in a delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
notes.E: The antibody-based description is false, but the role of Th1 signalling in delayed inflammation is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Many steroid hormones change transcription of target genes.
Reason: Steroid hormones are biosynthesized from cholesterol.
questions.why: Steroid hormones derive from cholesterol, and many regulate transcription. Genomic regulation occurs through hormone-bound steroid receptors acting at target regulatory regions, rather than following simply from the biosynthetic precursor.

notes.A: Cholesterol supplies the steroid scaffold, but receptor interactions with regulatory DNA and cofactors explain the transcriptional response.
notes.C: Cholesterol is indeed the common precursor of steroid hormones.
notes.D: Nuclear receptor signalling allows many steroids to regulate transcription, so the assertion is true.
notes.E: Both the source of steroid hormones and the ability of many to change transcription are established.

questions.stem:
Assertion: DNA polymerases extend daughter DNA strands in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction.
Reason: Replicative DNA polymerases can initiate synthesis without any primer.
questions.why: DNA polymerase adds each nucleotide to a free 3′ hydroxyl, producing 5′ to 3′ extension. Replicative polymerases need a primer that supplies that hydroxyl.

notes.A: Daughter strands do grow 5′ to 3′, but replicative polymerases cannot normally initiate without a primer.
notes.B: The primer requirement is essential to extension, so the second claim is false rather than an independent truth.
notes.D: Replicative polymerase does extend new DNA 5′ to 3′ and needs an available 3′ hydroxyl for addition.
notes.E: The primer-free claim is false, but the stated direction of daughter-strand growth is correct.

questions.stem:
Assertion: RNA is more resistant than DNA to alkaline hydrolysis.
Reason: The ribose 2-prime hydroxyl can participate in cleavage of RNA phosphodiester bonds.
questions.why: RNA is more susceptible to alkaline hydrolysis than DNA. Under alkaline conditions its 2′ hydroxyl can attack the adjacent phosphate and promote cleavage of the RNA backbone.

notes.A: The 2′ hydroxyl facilitates cleavage and therefore makes RNA less resistant to alkali, contrary to the assertion.
notes.B: The ability of the ribose hydroxyl to participate in cleavage is real, while the stated comparison of resistance is reversed.
notes.C: RNA is less resistant to alkaline hydrolysis, and intramolecular attack by the 2′ hydroxyl helps explain this.
notes.E: The resistance comparison is false, but the 2′ hydroxyl does participate in backbone cleavage.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Histone acetylation silences all nearby genes.
Reason: Lysine acetylation increases the positive charge on histone tails.
questions.why: Acetylation of lysine neutralises its positive charge. Histone acetylation is generally associated with more accessible chromatin, so the statements about universal silencing and increased charge are both false.

notes.A: Acetylation can increase chromatin accessibility and does not add positive charge to lysine.
notes.B: The two claims are not valid independent facts. Acetylation neutralises charge and does not universally silence nearby genes.
notes.C: Nearby genes are not uniformly silenced by a modification generally associated with accessible chromatin.
notes.D: Acetylating the lysine amino group removes its positive charge rather than increasing it.

questions.stem:
Which events follow light activation of rhodopsin?
I. Metarhodopsin II can activate transducin.
II. Activated phosphodiesterase raises cGMP.
III. Closure of cation channels hyperpolarizes rods.
questions.why: Metarhodopsin II activates transducin, which stimulates phosphodiesterase to lower cGMP. Closure of cGMP-gated cation channels then reduces inward current and hyperpolarises the rod.

notes.A: The statement about cGMP is false because activated phosphodiesterase hydrolyses the nucleotide.
notes.B: The combination includes the incorrect rise in cGMP and leaves out the resulting hyperpolarisation of the rod.
notes.C: Metarhodopsin II does activate transducin, whereas the assertion that phosphodiesterase raises cGMP is false.
notes.E: Metarhodopsin II activates transducin, but channel closure and resulting rod hyperpolarisation are also correct.

questions.stem:
Which statements about collagen processing are correct?
I. Hydroxyproline helps stabilize the triple helix.
II. Hydroxylation occurs before mature helix formation.
III. Lysyl oxidase acts within the cell nucleus.
questions.why: Hydroxylases act on collagen chains before stable triple-helix assembly, and hydroxyproline helps stabilise the helix. Lysyl oxidase acts outside the cell to initiate cross-linking.

notes.A: The first two statements are correct, but lysyl oxidase does not perform collagen cross-linking inside the nucleus.
notes.C: Hydroxylation precedes helix formation, but the included claim about nuclear lysyl oxidase is false.
notes.D: Hydroxyproline does stabilise the helix, but lysyl oxidase acts in extracellular cross-linking and not in the nucleus.
notes.E: This leaves out the true statement that hydroxylation occurs before assembly of a stable triple helix.

questions.stem:
Consider the following immune-system statements:
I. IgM is actively transported across the placenta.
II. C3b supports opsonophagocytosis.
III. C5a promotes leukocyte recruitment.
questions.why: Placental transport chiefly supplies maternal IgG rather than IgM. C3b marks targets for phagocyte recognition, and C5a is a soluble mediator that recruits leukocytes.

notes.A: It is IgG that crosses the placenta through a specific transport route, so the IgM statement is false.
notes.B: C3b supports opsonisation, but IgM is not the actively transported placental class and C5a also recruits leukocytes.
notes.D: C5a does promote recruitment, but the IgM claim is false and C3b also supports phagocytosis.
notes.E: The selected statement is false because placental transfer principally supplies maternal IgG.

questions.stem:
Which are characteristic of a sensitized mast cell's response to allergen re-exposure?
I. Surface IgE can be cross-linked.
II. Histamine can be released rapidly.
III. Newly made leukotrienes can contribute to inflammation.
questions.why: Re-exposure can cross-link IgE already bound to mast-cell receptors, releasing preformed histamine. Mast cells also synthesise leukotrienes, which contribute to the ensuing inflammation.

notes.B: The combination omits newly synthesised leukotrienes, which can contribute to the inflammatory response.
notes.C: Histamine release and leukotriene synthesis both occur, but they can follow cross-linking of surface IgE.
notes.D: The selected events are correct, but mast cells also release preformed histamine rapidly.
notes.E: IgE cross-linking is an initiating event. The response also includes histamine release and synthesis of lipid mediators.

questions.stem:
Which statements about hormone classes are correct?
I. Peptide hormones commonly bind cell-surface receptors.
II. Steroid hormones all signal exclusively through IP3.
III. ACTH is a catecholamine derived from tyrosine.
questions.why: Peptide hormones generally signal through cell-surface receptors. Many steroids act through intracellular receptors, and ACTH is a pituitary peptide derived from a larger precursor protein.

notes.A: The steroid and ACTH statements are false because classical steroids act genomically and ACTH is a peptide.
notes.B: The peptide hormone statement is correct, but steroids do not all use signalling through IP3.
notes.C: Neither the exclusive IP3 claim nor the description of ACTH as a catecholamine is correct.
notes.D: ACTH is a peptide produced from proopiomelanocortin, so the proposed catecholamine classification is incorrect.

questions.stem:
Which are common features of eukaryotic pre-mRNA maturation?
I. Removal of introns by splicing.
II. Addition of a protective poly-A tail.
III. DNA polymerase III creates the 5-prime RNA cap.
questions.why: Eukaryotic precursor mRNA commonly undergoes splicing and addition of a poly-A tail. Its 5′ cap is attached by RNA-capping enzymes rather than by a replicative DNA polymerase.

notes.A: The first two events are genuine, but DNA polymerase III does not catalyse RNA capping.
notes.C: Polyadenylation is correct, but capping requires RNA-processing enzymes and introns are also removed by splicing.
notes.D: Splicing is correct, but the proposed DNA polymerase does not cap RNA.
notes.E: Removing introns is correct, and polyadenylation also contributes to maturation of many eukaryotic messages.

questions.stem:
Which statements about a DNA replication fork are correct?
I. Helicase unwinds the parental duplex.
II. Primase supplies short RNA primers.
III. Ligase seals DNA backbone nicks.
questions.why: Helicase separates parental strands, primase supplies RNA primers and ligase seals backbone nicks after fragment processing. Each activity supports a different step of replication.

notes.B: Helicase and primase perform their stated roles, but the set omits ligase, which seals the backbone.
notes.C: Primer synthesis and nick sealing are both correct, but helicase also unwinds the parental duplex.
notes.D: Both selected activities occur, but primase also provides the starting RNA primers.
notes.E: Helicase unwinds the duplex, and replication also requires priming and removal of backbone discontinuities.
